title: The fifteen-minute city
summary_es: Qué es la ciudad de los quince minutos, qué ventajas le ven sus defensores y qué objeciones serias plantean sus críticos.
prediction_prompt: Could you reach everything you need in fifteen minutes on foot? Would you like to?

sentences.text: Imagine being able to reach your office, your children's school, a doctor, a park and a decent supermarket within a quarter of an hour, without ever starting an engine.
That is the promise of the so-called fifteen-minute city, an idea that has moved in less than a decade from academic papers to the election programmes of mayors around the world.
The concept is not complicated.
Instead of dividing a city into zones, with housing in one place, offices in another and shopping somewhere else, planners try to mix them.
Every neighbourhood should contain most of what its residents need for daily life, and they should be able to reach all of it on foot or by bicycle.
In a sense, it is a return to the way cities worked before the car reorganised them.
Supporters point to obvious benefits.
Shorter journeys mean less traffic and cleaner air.
People who walk more tend to be healthier, and streets with more pedestrians are generally safer and better for small businesses.
There is also the question of time.
The average commuter in a large European city spends the equivalent of several working weeks every year simply travelling to and from work.
Had those hours been spent differently, the argument goes, both families and local communities would be stronger.
Paris is the example most often quoted.
Over the past few years the city has built hundreds of kilometres of cycle lanes, closed streets near schools to traffic and turned parking spaces into gardens.
Cycling has grown dramatically as a result.
Other cities, from Melbourne to Bogotá, have adopted similar plans under different names.
Nevertheless, the idea has its critics, and not all of their objections are unreasonable.
The first concerns inequality.
Neighbourhoods that become greener and quieter also tend to become more expensive, so the people who were supposed to benefit may be pushed out by rising rents.
A fifteen-minute city that only the wealthy can afford would be a strange kind of progress.
A second objection is practical.
Many jobs cannot be moved closer to where people live.
Not everyone can work from a desk at home.
A hospital, a factory or an airport serves a whole region, and those who work there will continue to need fast transport across the city.
Critics argue that money spent on local streets is money not spent on trains and buses.
Finally, some residents simply distrust the motives behind the plans.
Whenever a street is closed to cars, a few people see it as an attempt to control where they go, although nothing in the proposals prevents anyone from travelling as far as they wish.
The most reasonable conclusion is probably a modest one.
The fifteen-minute city is not a miracle, and it cannot be applied in the same way to a medieval centre and to a suburb built for cars.
But as a direction of travel, rather than a rigid rule, it asks a question worth asking: who, and what, should our streets be for?

language_focus.explanation_es: *Had those hours been spent differently* = *If those hours had been spent differently*. Es una inversión formal, frecuente en textos escritos y en el Use of English.
*Nevertheless* abre la parte crítica del texto; *although* concede un punto dentro de la frase; *rather than* contrapone dos opciones.

tasks.prompt: Which sentence best summarises the article?

options.text: The fifteen-minute city has failed wherever it has been tried
The fifteen-minute city is a promising idea with real limits
The fifteen-minute city is mainly about banning cars
The fifteen-minute city only works in Paris

tasks.rationale_es: Presenta ventajas y objeciones, y concluye que es una buena dirección, no una receta.

tasks.prompt: Match paragraphs 3, 5, 6 and 7 with the best heading. There is one extra heading.
tasks.rationale_es: El párrafo 3 reúne los argumentos a favor; el 5, la desigualdad; el 6, los trabajos que no se pueden acercar; el 7, la desconfianza. De turistas no se habla.

tasks.prompt: According to paragraph 2, how do fifteen-minute cities differ from traditional planning?

options.text: They separate homes from workplaces more strictly
They combine different uses in the same area
They build more roads
They move shops to the suburbs

tasks.rationale_es: En vez de separar vivienda, oficinas y tiendas por zonas, las mezclan.

tasks.prompt: In paragraph 3, "the argument goes" shows that the writer is…

options.text: reporting what supporters claim
giving a strong personal opinion
correcting a mistake
quoting a law

tasks.rationale_es: Con *the argument goes* el autor atribuye la idea a los defensores, sin hacerla suya.

tasks.prompt: In Paris, some space that used to belong to cars is now used for other things.
tasks.rationale_es: Calles cerradas al tráfico y aparcamientos convertidos en jardines.

options.text: Rich areas will refuse to change
Poor areas have too many cars already
Improvements may push up housing costs for locals
Cyclists pay less tax

tasks.rationale_es: Los barrios mejorados se encarecen y pueden expulsar a quienes debían beneficiarse.

tasks.prompt: In paragraph 6, "those who work there" refers to people who work…

options.text: in local shops
in city planning offices
at home
in places such as hospitals and airports

tasks.rationale_es: *There* recoge *a hospital, a factory or an airport*.

tasks.prompt: What does the writer imply about people who distrust the plans?

options.text: Their fear is not supported by the actual proposals
They are completely right to be worried about them
They should be forced to cycle
They mostly live in Paris

tasks.rationale_es: El *although* lo deja claro: nada en las propuestas impide a nadie viajar adonde quiera.

tasks.prompt: The writer believes the same plan can be used in every type of neighbourhood.
tasks.rationale_es: No se puede aplicar igual a un centro medieval que a un barrio pensado para el coche.

tasks.prompt: What is the writer's overall attitude to the idea?

options.text: Enthusiastic and uncritical
Hostile
Cautiously positive
Indifferent

tasks.rationale_es: Reconoce los límites, pero cree que la pregunta que plantea merece la pena.

tasks.prompt: Why does the article end with a question?

options.text: To show that the writer has no opinion at all on the matter
To suggest the topic is too complex to discuss
To criticise mayors
To invite readers to think about what streets are for

tasks.rationale_es: Cierra dejando al lector la pregunta de fondo: para quién y para qué son las calles.

tasks.prompt: Most residents of Paris support the changes.
tasks.rationale_es: El texto cuenta qué se ha hecho en París y que el ciclismo ha crecido, pero no dice qué opinan sus vecinos.

tasks.prompt: Complete with one word from the text in each gap.
tasks.text: Greener neighbourhoods {{1}} to become more expensive. The idea is a direction of travel {{2}} than a rigid rule.
tasks.rationale_es: *Tend to* = soler; *rather than* = en lugar de, más que.
